classification.difficultyReason: Nine direct single-bracket expansions, including negative multipliers and an implicit multiplier of −1.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 assesses the single-bracket distributive law from page 2; parts c–i additionally require signed multiplication, with an implicit multiplier of −1 in g–i. Two-bracket and special-product methods are unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states a(x+y)=ax+ay and Example 1 distributes the outside multiplier to each term, retaining product signs. Page 3 develops expansion of two brackets and special products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Nine direct single-bracket expansions, including negative multipliers and an implicit multiplier of −1.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct distribution of a numerical or algebraic multiplier across one bracket, including negative multipliers.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–i directly applies single-bracket distribution; b, e, f and h require negative product signs, and d–f and i require multiplication of pronumerals. No binomial-product or special-expansion method is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 gives the distributive identities a(x+y)=ax+ay and (x+y)a=xa+ya. Example 1 distributes numerical and algebraic multipliers, retaining product signs and simplifying terms. Page 3 continues expansion and collection methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct distribution of a numerical or algebraic multiplier across one bracket, including negative multipliers.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law, including negative multipliers, and collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess single-bracket expansion followed by collecting like terms. Parts with a subtracted bracket require distributing its negative multiplier; no binomial-product identity is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces collecting like terms and the distributive law. Example 1 expands each bracket, retains the signs of products and then combines like terms; page 3 continues expansion methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law, including negative multipliers, and collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law to two binomials and collect like terms, including negative coefficients and different pronumerals.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess binomial expansion using Example 2's method; part l retains two distinct pronumerals and therefore has four unlike terms.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces distribution and collecting like terms. Example 2 on page 3 distributes each term of the first bracket across the second bracket, expands each product, then collects like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law to two binomials and collect like terms, including negative coefficients and different pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: The expansion route and target identities are supplied; proving each requires direct distribution and collection of like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly requires proofs of the square of a sum, square of a difference and difference of squares, matching special-products.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 gives the distributive law. Page 3 Example 2 expands one bracket through the other and collects like terms; the Special expansions box states the three identities to be proved.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The expansion route and target identities are supplied; proving each requires direct distribution and collection of like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the matching taught identity and directly substitute each pair of terms; coefficients require routine multiplication and squaring.

questions.mappingNote: All 24 parts directly apply those three identities. Parts a, d, f, i, l, m, o, p, s and w use the square of a sum; b, e, j, n, t, v and x use the square of a difference; c, g, h, k, q, r and u use the difference of squares. The supplied reuse candidates concern different complete tasks and are inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces distribution and collecting like terms. Page 3 states the square-of-a-sum, square-of-a-difference and difference-of-squares identities; Example 3 applies each directly, including squaring a coefficient with its variable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the matching taught identity and directly substitute each pair of terms; coefficients require routine multiplication and squaring.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the familiar identities with terms t and 1/t, simplifying their product and the square of the reciprocal.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and c respectively apply these three identities with A=t and B=1/t; simplifying t(1/t) gives the constant middle term in a and b.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 demonstrates distribution and collecting like terms. Page 3 states the square-of-a-sum, square-of-a-difference and difference-of-squares identities, and Example 3 applies each directly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the familiar identities with terms t and 1/t, simplifying their product and the square of the reciprocal.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite numerical quantities around convenient powers of ten and apply the three special expansions without a calculator.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and c respectively apply those three identities to numerical calculations; special-products is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 demonstrates numerical partitioning before expansion. Page 3 supplies the square-of-a-sum, square-of-a-difference and difference-of-squares identities and demonstrates their application in Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rewrite numerical quantities around convenient powers of ten and apply the three special expansions without a calculator.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine distributive expansion and special products, then collect cancelling terms in expressions involving several variables and cubic powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and e extend Example 2 to cubic products; b and c combine the special expansions from Example 3; d combines two binomial products; f applies the square-of-a-sum identity with a grouped term and cancels like terms. The most advanced shared assessed skill is expanding and simplifying combinations of special products.
questions.methodNote: Use distribution as in Examples 1 and 2, then collect like terms. Apply the square-of-a-sum, square-of-a-difference and difference-of-squares identities from page 3; expand a cube as a square multiplied by the remaining bracket.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine distributive expansion and special products, then collect cancelling terms in expressions involving several variables and cubic powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply familiar expansions and repeated distribution, then collect terms; conjugate grouping is useful in part c but is not required.

questions.mappingNote: Part a expands a square before multiplying by the remaining bracket; b expands nested sums and cancels mixed terms; c recognises conjugate brackets with y-z as one term; d distributes three terms and collects cancellations. The closest directly assessed skill is expanding and simplifying combinations of special products.
questions.methodNote: Distribute each term across the other bracket, then collect like terms, following Examples 1 and 2. Use the square-of-a-sum, square-of-a-difference and difference-of-squares identities from page 3 where applicable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply familiar expansions and repeated distribution, then collect terms; conjugate grouping is useful in part c but is not required.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate ordered subtraction and a product of substituted expressions into algebra, then expand and collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies signed expansion to a worded subtraction; part b forms two sums before subtracting and simplifying; part c substitutes the supplied definitions before multiplying the resulting binomials. The existing expansion-and-factorisation problems skill is the closest overall match.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 demonstrates distributing a multiplier across every term, handling subtraction and collecting like terms. Page 3 demonstrates expanding two bracketed factors in successive steps and collecting like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate ordered subtraction and a product of substituted expressions into algebra, then expand and collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that squaring the given reciprocal sum determines the required expression without solving for x.

questions.mappingNote: The given reciprocal sum is the binomial to square; its cross-product is 2, leaving the requested sum of squares.
questions.methodNote: Use the square-of-a-sum identity on page 3, then collect terms as demonstrated on pages 2–3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that squaring the given reciprocal sum determines the required expression without solving for x.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand both sides using distributivity and square identities, cancel mixed terms and compare the collected expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies successive distributive expansions to both sides. Part b applies the two square identities and cancels opposite mixed terms before comparing with the expanded right side.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 distributes a multiplier over each term and collects like terms. Page 3 expands successive bracketed factors and gives the square-of-a-sum and square-of-a-difference identities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand both sides using distributivity and square identities, cancel mixed terms and compare the collected expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that rearranging the given equality produces a sum of three non-negative squares, then use its equality condition.

questions.mappingNote: The equality reduces to a sum of squares equal to zero; non-negativity supplies the proof that the four quantities are equal.
questions.methodNote: Expand brackets, collect like terms, and recognise squares of differences using the special expansions on page 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that rearranging the given equality produces a sum of three non-negative squares, then use its equality condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct extraction of a highest common numerical or algebraic factor, including powers and two variables.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess extracting a common factor. Parts a–b use numerical factors; c uses an algebraic factor; d and g–i combine numerical and algebraic factors; e–f involve a shared variable across different terms; j requires recognising ab despite written factor order; k–l require the lowest shared powers.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 Example 4 identifies the HCF and writes the expression as that factor multiplied by the remaining bracket. Pages 7–8 reinforce taking out common factors before further factorisation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct extraction of a highest common numerical or algebraic factor, including powers and two variables.

classification.difficultyReason: Applies the explicitly requested grouping method to four-term expressions.

questions.mappingNote: Every part contains four terms arranged into pairs with a common binomial; factorise-special-products explicitly includes grouping.
questions.methodNote: Factor each pair, then extract the common binomial, following page 8 Example 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies the explicitly requested grouping method to four-term expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the difference of squares, including squared algebraic terms.

questions.mappingNote: All sixteen parts are differences of two squares; the selected skill directly includes this factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Recognise A²−B² and write (A−B)(A+B), following pages 6–7 and Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the difference of squares, including squared algebraic terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly applies the taught sum-and-product method to explicitly identified monic quadratics, choosing signed integer factor pairs.

questions.mappingNote: All twenty-four expressions are monic quadratic trinomials, matching factorise-monic-quadratic exactly.
questions.methodNote: Find two numbers whose sum is the linear coefficient and whose product is the constant, following page 7 Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly applies the taught sum-and-product method to explicitly identified monic quadratics, choosing signed integer factor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognises explicitly identified perfect-square trinomials using half the linear coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses recognition and factorisation of a perfect-square trinomial; factorise-special-products is the closest factorisation skill.
questions.methodNote: Use A²±2AB+B²=(A±B)², checking that half the linear coefficient squares to the constant, as taught on page 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognises explicitly identified perfect-square trinomials using half the linear coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: The supplied binomial scaffold directly cues halving the linear coefficient and squaring it; fractional halves introduce no additional conceptual decision.

questions.mappingNote: Every part completes a monic perfect-square identity. Completing the square is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill; exact fractional halves are retained in e, f and h.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 teaches recognising perfect squares using A² ± 2AB + B² = (A ± B)², and explicitly halves the linear coefficient then squares it to obtain the constant.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The supplied binomial scaffold directly cues halving the linear coefficient and squaring it; fractional halves introduce no additional conceptual decision.

classification.difficultyReason: Source Foundation exercise: apply middle-term splitting and grouping to non-monic quadratic trinomials.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses non-monic trinomial factorisation; factorise-special-products explicitly includes non-monic trinomials. All worked answers use the source's splitting-and-grouping method.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 on pages 7–8 selects two numbers with sum b and product ac, splits the middle term, takes the HCF of each pair, then extracts the common binomial.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Source Foundation exercise: apply middle-term splitting and grouping to non-monic quadratic trinomials.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and apply HCF, special products, quadratic factoring and grouping across mixed expressions.

questions.mappingNote: This mixed set directly combines the four methods taught on pages 6–8.
questions.methodNote: Take out common factors first; use difference of squares, sum/product factoring, splitting the middle term, perfect squares and grouping.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and apply HCF, special products, quadratic factoring and grouping across mixed expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires successive factoring methods and recognising when factors can be factored further.

questions.mappingNote: The instruction to factor fully directly applies the irreducible-factor stopping rule on page 6.
questions.methodNote: Extract the HCF first, group where needed, then continue factoring using quadratic factors and differences of squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires successive factoring methods and recognising when factors can be factored further.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines compound squares, grouping, quadratic substitution and multiple factoring stages.

questions.mappingNote: Extends the taught factoring identities to higher powers and compound binomials without introducing polynomial division.
questions.methodNote: Use HCF, grouping, split middle terms and recognise compound differences of squares.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines compound squares, grouping, quadratic substitution and multiple factoring stages.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires strategic regrouping, recognising compound factors and adding and subtracting terms to create differences of squares.

questions.mappingNote: These enrichment tasks extend the same identities and grouping methods; the answer evidence explicitly supplies the add-and-subtract strategy for g and h.
questions.methodNote: Use grouping, perfect-square recognition, expansion and differences of squares; strategically add and subtract terms for parts g and h.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires strategic regrouping, recognising compound factors and adding and subtracting terms to create differences of squares.

classification.difficultyReason: The Enrichment proof requires arranging a multivariable expression into a sum of squares and justifying when both squares vanish.

questions.mappingNote: Completing squares is explicitly required by this question; complete-square-form is the closest existing skill. The final deduction uses the non-negativity of real squares.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 supplies the perfect-square identity A²−2AB+B²=(A−B)². Complete two squares, then use non-negativity to establish equality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The Enrichment proof requires arranging a multivariable expression into a sum of squares and justifying when both squares vanish.

classification.difficultyReason: Cancel common numerical and variable factors in six single algebraic fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c cancel a common x; part d cancels one factor a; parts e–f cancel numerical and variable factors, including repeated variable factors. All six directly assess simplification of algebraic fractions.
questions.methodNote: Factor numerators and denominators, then cancel common factors, following Key Idea 4 and Examples 9 and 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Cancel common numerical and variable factors in six single algebraic fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Routine multiplication and division of monomial fractions using reciprocals and cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, c, d, e and g multiply monomial fractions and cancel numerical or variable factors. Parts b, f and h first use the reciprocal. The selected skill directly covers operations with pronumerals in denominators.
questions.methodNote: Cancel common factors in products; replace division by multiplication by the reciprocal, following Key Idea 6 and Example 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Routine multiplication and division of monomial fractions using reciprocals and cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise requires common numerical denominators and collection of like terms.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess addition or subtraction of algebraic fractions with numerical denominators; no factorisation of algebraic denominators is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the lowest common denominator, combine numerators and cancel common numerical factors where necessary, following Key Ideas 5 and Example 10 on page 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise requires common numerical denominators and collection of like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: The source places this question before the Development boundary. Each part requires combining two fractions with equal or simple related algebraic denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b already share denominators. Parts c–f require common denominators 2a, 6x, 12a and 6x respectively; part f then requires cancellation. This directly assesses operations with pronumerals in denominators.
questions.methodNote: Key Idea 5 and Example 10 teach rewriting fractions with the lowest common denominator, combining their numerators, then cancelling common factors if necessary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source places this question before the Development boundary. Each part requires combining two fractions with equal or simple related algebraic denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise requires common numerical denominators, expansion of binomial numerators and collection of like terms.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess adding or subtracting fractions with binomial numerators and numerical denominators; no denominator factorisation or compound-fraction method is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 instructs use of the lowest common denominator and cancellation where necessary. Page 12, Examples 10 and 11, demonstrates combining numerators over a common denominator, expanding subtraction correctly and simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise requires common numerical denominators, expansion of binomial numerators and collection of like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise requires common-factor, quadratic and special-product factorisation followed by cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess simplification by factorisation; later parts use difference of squares, perfect squares and monic quadratic factors. The supplied reuse candidates contain different complete tasks and are inapplicable.
questions.methodNote: Factor numerator and denominator completely, then cancel common factors, following Key Idea 4 and Example 9 on page 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source Foundation exercise requires common-factor, quadratic and special-product factorisation followed by cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: The source Development question requires constructing common binomial denominators and correctly expanding subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess addition or subtraction with pronumerals in denominators. Distinct linear factors supply the common denominator; no preliminary quadratic factorisation is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 prescribes a lowest common denominator and cancellation where necessary. Page 12 Examples 10d and 11 demonstrate combining binomial denominators, preserving brackets during subtraction, then simplifying the numerator. Page 13 was inspected and concerns multiplication, division and compound fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The source Development question requires constructing common binomial denominators and correctly expanding subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Select familiar factorisations, convert each division to reciprocal multiplication and cancel factors, including grouping in part e and successive divisions in part f.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess products or quotients simplified by factorisation. Parts a and b use common and quadratic factors; c adds reciprocal multiplication; d combines three fractions; e requires grouping and special products; f requires reciprocal multiplication for both successive divisors. The closest catalogue skill is simplify-fractions-by-factorising.
questions.methodNote: Key Ideas 4 and 6 and Example 12 teach complete factorisation, multiplication by a divisor's reciprocal and cancellation of common factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select familiar factorisations, convert each division to reciprocal multiplication and cancel factors, including grouping in part e and successive divisions in part f.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise opposite binomial factors, factorise quadratic expressions and combine fractions with opposite denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c use opposite factors and cancellation; d–e combine fractions after reversing a denominator's sign; f factorises a quadratic denominator before cancelling an opposite factor. These directly assess simplification by factorising.
questions.methodNote: Factor numerators and denominators completely before cancelling; rewrite opposite binomials using a negative factor; use a common denominator before combining fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise opposite binomial factors, factorise quadratic expressions and combine fractions with opposite denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor quadratic denominators, construct common denominators and simplify sums involving up to three fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Example 11 directly models factoring before subtraction; Examples 9–10 support cancellation and common denominators.
questions.methodNote: Factor denominators completely, use the lowest common denominator, combine numerators and cancel common factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor quadratic denominators, construct common denominators and simplify sums involving up to three fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Select common multiples to clear nested numerical and algebraic fractions, then simplify.

questions.mappingNote: Key idea 7 and Example 13 teach precisely the compound-fraction method required by all ten parts.
questions.methodNote: Multiply the top and bottom by the lowest common multiple of their internal denominators, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select common multiples to clear nested numerical and algebraic fractions, then simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute through three linked expressions and simplify compound fractions to establish the identity.

questions.mappingNote: Example 13 and key idea 7 support simplifying the compound fractions after each substitution.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the supplied expressions and clear internal denominators by multiplying top and bottom by their common denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute through three linked expressions and simplify compound fractions to establish the identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Select factorisations, reverse the divisor and coordinate common denominators; all four parts use routine linked applications of the taught methods.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply Example 12 with multiple factorisations. Parts c and d apply Examples 10 and 11, including subtraction of complete numerators. Factorisation is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Factor numerators and denominators completely before cancelling; replace division by reciprocal multiplication; use a lowest common denominator for addition and subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select factorisations, reverse the divisor and coordinate common denominators; all four parts use routine linked applications of the taught methods.

classification.difficultyReason: Decompose nested fractions, manage reversed-factor signs and combine common denominators with reciprocal multiplication; these are extended routine procedures without an essential unsignposted insight.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply the common-denominator and factorisation methods from pages 11–12. Parts c and d combine those methods with the compound-fraction and reciprocal methods on page 13. The most advanced directly assessed skill is simplifying compound fractions.
questions.methodNote: Factor numerators and denominators completely; add or subtract using the lowest common denominator; clear compound fractions by multiplying numerator and denominator by the LCD; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal before cancelling.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Decompose nested fractions, manage reversed-factor signs and combine common denominators with reciprocal multiplication; these are extended routine procedures without an essential unsignposted insight.

classification.difficultyReason: Isolate a squared variable and take both square roots; the later parts require division and fractional roots.

questions.mappingNote: Each part reduces directly to a positive equation of the form av²=c. Solving these equations, including fractional roots, is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply the same operation to both sides to isolate the square, then retain both positive and negative square roots, as demonstrated in Example 16.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Isolate a squared variable and take both square roots; the later parts require division and fractional roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract a common pronumeral factor and apply the null factor law, rearranging some equations first.

questions.mappingNote: Each assigned equation factors by extracting its pronumeral; parts e, f, j and k first require rearrangement. Completing the square and the formula on pages 17–18 are not required by this instruction.
questions.methodNote: Page 16 Key Idea 8 and Example 14: collect all terms on the left, factor the left-hand side, then set each factor equal to zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract a common pronumeral factor and apply the null factor law, rearranging some equations first.

classification.difficultyReason: Routine monic quadratic factorisation and the null factor law, including rearrangement and a repeated root.

questions.mappingNote: All eighteen parts are monic quadratics with integer factors. Parts j–p and r require collecting terms on the left; q benefits from ordering terms. The directly assessed skill is solving monic quadratics by factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Page 16, Key Idea 8 and Example 14: collect all terms on the left, factor the left-hand side, then set each factor equal to zero. Page 18 illustrates recording a repeated root once.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Routine monic quadratic factorisation and the null factor law, including rearrangement and a repeated root.

classification.difficultyReason: Routine non-monic quadratic factorisation and the null factor law, including rearrangement and a repeated root.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part is a non-monic quadratic with rational roots. The requested factoring method directly matches Example 14; part o has an identical repeated factor.
questions.methodNote: Page 16, Key Idea 8 and Example 14: rearrange to zero, split the middle term, factor by grouping and set each factor equal to zero. Pages 17–18 establish that a perfect-square equation can have one solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Routine non-monic quadratic factorisation and the null factor law, including rearrangement and a repeated root.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the prescribed quadratic formula, rearranging some equations first, simplifying exact roots and rounding irrational roots to four significant figures.

questions.mappingNote: Every part explicitly requires the quadratic formula; parts b, c, g, i, j and k first require standard form. Four-significant-figure approximations apply to irrational real roots.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 Key Idea 11 and Example 17 calculate the discriminant first, substitute into the quadratic formula, simplify surds and identify repeated or absent real roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the prescribed quadratic formula, rearranging some equations first, simplifying exact roots and rounding irrational roots to four significant figures.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified completing-the-square procedure to monic quadratics, including fractional halves, surd solutions and a negative square.

questions.mappingNote: Every part explicitly requests completing the square; complete-the-square-solve directly matches the assessed method, including fractional coefficients and the no-real-solution case.
questions.methodNote: Following Key Ideas 9–10 and Example 16, move the constant to the right, add the square of half the linear coefficient to both sides, write a perfect square, and take both square roots. Example 16d establishes that a negative square gives no real solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the specified completing-the-square procedure to monic quadratics, including fractional halves, surd solutions and a negative square.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear variable denominators or expand a product before rearranging and factoring a quadratic.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess solving quadratics by factoring; variable-denominator manipulation is preparatory in a–c. Completing the square and the formula are inspected context but are not the requested method.
questions.methodNote: Follow page 16: rearrange with zero on the right, factor the left-hand side and apply the null factor law. Clear nonzero denominators first in a–c; split the middle term and group for non-monic quadratics, as in Example 14.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear variable denominators or expand a product before rearranging and factoring a quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Clear algebraic denominators, form quadratics and obtain exact surd solutions while retaining denominator restrictions.

questions.mappingNote: All four rational equations become quadratics with irrational exact roots. Completing the square is the directly assessed solving skill used here; clearing algebraic denominators is a prerequisite.
questions.methodNote: Clear nonzero denominators using the equation principles on page 16, then complete the square by halving the linear coefficient and adding its square to both sides, as in Example 16 on pages 17–18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Clear algebraic denominators, form quadratics and obtain exact surd solutions while retaining denominator restrictions.

classification.difficultyReason: The method is specified, but students must normalise non-monic quadratics, complete squares using fractions and recognise a negative square as giving no real solution.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts explicitly assess completing the square after division by a non-unit quadratic coefficient; the selected skill directly matches that required method.
questions.methodNote: Key Idea 10 and Example 16 prescribe dividing by the quadratic coefficient, adding the square of half the linear coefficient to both sides, rewriting as a square and taking both square roots. Example 16d treats a negative square as having no real solutions.
